title: The doctrine of salvation
for: I want to understand how God saves
subtitle: Eleven sessions on how God saves, from the image and the fall through grace, election, new birth, justification, adoption and holiness, to explaining grace to someone who thinks they must earn it.
intro: The church has a name for the doctrine of how God saves: soteriology. These sessions take it a piece at a time, from what was lost in the fall to what is given in Christ, and each one asks you to do four things: say the doctrine in your own words, find where it comes from in Scripture, see why the church has held it, and explain it simply to someone else.

Salvation by grace, through the cross, as God's own act, is confessed plainly here, because every great tradition confesses it. How election works, how the new birth relates to faith and baptism, and whether a believer can fall away are questions that divide faithful churches, and each view is given in its own strongest voice and left open. The author is a Baptist pastor and says so where it helps, without arguing for it.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through The doctrine of salvation. The group suits Christians who want to understand what they believe about how God saves and why, and it welcomes anyone from outside the faith who wants to hear the doctrine from the inside. The leader's task is to keep the group in Scripture, to confess plainly what the creeds and every great tradition confess, and to give room where faithful churches differ.

Each person reads the session, opens its page and does what it asks before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for eleven meetings, and keep the end time you promised. The doctrine pages are long, so say at the start that no one needs to read every word, only enough to bring one thing they noticed and one question. A leader doesn't need to be a theologian. A leader needs to have done the reading and to be willing to say that they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: A table works best, with Bibles open in front of everyone and paper for notes. Say at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that the group will disagree about some things and that this is allowed, and that no one has to pray aloud. If the group includes people from different churches, name that as a gift: the sessions on election, new birth and perseverance are richer with more than one tradition in the room. What people say about their own lives stays in the room, unless someone is in danger.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and the passage around it, while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is found, in Scripture or on the page.
Ten minutes: each person states the session's doctrine in a sentence of their own, as if to a friend.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in the group's own words.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: First ask what order the question is. Salvation by grace, through Christ's death and resurrection, as God's own work, is first-order, and the sessions say so plainly. How God's choosing relates to human choosing, whether new birth comes before faith, how baptism relates to new birth, and whether a believer can fall away are second-order. Faithful churches divide over them, and the group should leave them open.

Let each view be stated in a form its own defenders would accept before anyone argues against it. A good test is whether a Calvinist and a Wesleyan in the room would each say their view was stated well. If no one knows the answer, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: The doctrine of salvation touches tender places. A session on sin can land on someone who cannot stop punishing themselves, a session on election can frighten someone who fears they are not chosen, and a session on adoption can open the wound of a father who was absent or cruel. When the study touches someone's life, stop and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't explain their pain for them, and don't hurry back to the outline. Speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the authorities, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: guilt or fear that will not let them rest for weeks, a conscience that keeps checking whether they have really believed, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Made in God's image, and fallen
teaching: Salvation means rescue, and rescue only makes sense once you know what was lost. The Bible's account of human beings begins high. Before anything goes wrong, God makes man and woman in his image and gives them the world to keep, and the psalmist marvels at it: “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:5). That dignity is the first fact about you, older than anything you've done. A doctrine of salvation that starts with what went wrong instead of with the image always ends up too small, because it forgets what God is restoring. He isn't salvaging spare parts. He is bringing home a son or a daughter.

Genesis 3 tells how that glory was bent. The first couple listen to a voice that questions God's goodness, reach for what was not given, and then hide. Trust is lost in every direction: with God, with each other, even with the ground. Yet the first thing God says after the fall is a question, not a sentence: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). The church has long read that as the first sign of what salvation will be. God comes looking. Christians differ on how to read the garden, but they confess together that humanity was made good and is now fallen, and that the image is defaced, not erased.

sessions.title: Sin and how far it reaches
teaching: Sin in Scripture is more than a list of wrong acts. It is a condition before it is a deed, a heart turned in on itself, and its reach is total in the old sense of that word: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that no part of them is untouched, mind, will, desire and body alike. Paul traces the condition to its source: “Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). The question the church has argued over for sixteen centuries is what exactly passed on from Adam, and how.

Augustine, followed by much of the Western church, held that Adam's children inherit both a corrupted nature and a share in his guilt, and Reformed theology added that Adam stood for humanity as Christ stands for his people. Wesleyans hold the same inherited corruption and stress the grace that reaches every person before they seek it. The Orthodox speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a bent toward sin, but not Adam's personal guilt. Many Baptists confess that we inherit a nature inclined toward sin and become guilty when we are able to choose and do sin. What every tradition rejects is the teaching of Pelagius, that we begin neutral and can choose the good by our own strength.

sessions.title: Grace
teaching: Grace is the hinge of the whole doctrine of salvation. It means God's favor toward people who have no claim on it, and in the New Testament it is never a vague mood. It is God himself acting in kindness. Paul refuses to let it be mixed with wages: “And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace” (Romans 11:6). The argument between Augustine and Pelagius early in the fifth century was finally an argument about that verse. Pelagius thought of grace as help for people already able to obey. Augustine, who knew his own will had been captive, insisted that grace is rescue.

Theologians distinguish kinds of grace, and the distinctions help. Common grace is the goodness God shows everyone: rain, beauty, conscience, the restraint of evil. Saving grace is his work of bringing people to himself. Wesleyans speak of prevenient grace, grace that goes before, freeing every person enough to respond. Catholic theology speaks of grace given through the sacraments that heals and raises human nature. Reformed theology speaks of grace that is effectual, that brings and does not only invite. They differ on how grace works. They agree on where it comes from: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (Titus 2:11). No tradition teaches that anyone saves themselves.

sessions.title: Election and predestination
teaching: Scripture speaks plainly of God choosing. Paul writes that God “chose us in Him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4) and that “it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy” (Romans 9:16). The same Scriptures say that God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), and they call every hearer to repent and believe. Every tradition has to hold both, and the great systems are different ways of holding them. This is a second-order question. Faithful churches divide over it, the creeds don't settle it, and it should be studied with humility on every side.

The Reformed view, confessed at the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, holds that God chose some unconditionally, out of mercy alone, and that his grace will surely bring them home; its strength is that salvation stays wholly God's gift. The Arminian view, from the Remonstrants of 1610 and later John Wesley, holds that God chose in Christ those he foresaw would believe, and that grace enables everyone to respond; its strength is that God's love is universal and the response real. Lutherans confess election to salvation but will not reason from it to a decree of damnation. Molinists appeal to God's knowledge of what every free creature would do. Karl Barth taught that Christ is the chosen one, and we are chosen in him. Baptists have stood on more than one of these sides.

sessions.title: The call and the new birth
teaching: The gospel goes out to everyone, and theologians call that the outward or general call: the invitation preached to all, and meant sincerely by God. But Jesus told Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, something no teacher can do for himself: “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3). The new birth, or regeneration, is the Spirit's work of giving a person new life, the new heart Ezekiel promised in place of a heart of stone. Birth is a good picture because no one arranges their own. You can hear a call, but life has to be given.

Christians differ on how the call and the new birth fit together. Reformed theology teaches an effectual call: the Spirit gives new life, and the person, made alive, freely believes, so new birth comes logically before faith. Wesleyans hold that prevenient grace enables a response that may be refused, and that new birth follows faith. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches join the new birth to baptism, where God acts through water and the word. Baptists, the author's own church among them, hold that the Spirit gives new birth through the word heard and believed, and that baptism follows as its sign. All agree it is God's work: “The wind blows where it wishes” (John 3:8).

sessions.title: Repentance and faith
teaching: When the new birth shows itself, it looks like two movements that are really one turning. Repentance turns away from sin; faith turns toward Christ. Paul summed up his preaching that way: “repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21). The New Testament word for repentance means a change of mind, but it doesn't stay in the mind. It reaches desire and action, and it is different from regret. Paul draws the line sharply: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Worldly sorrow grieves at being caught. Godly sorrow grieves at having wronged someone you love, and it turns home.

The older Protestant teachers described faith as three strands: knowing what the gospel says, agreeing that it is true, and trusting Christ himself with your whole weight. The first two without the third are not yet saving faith; James observes that even the demons believe and shudder. Christians have argued about which comes first, repentance or faith, and about how much a new believer must understand. Most traditions answer that they arrive together, and that both are gifts as well as acts: God grants repentance, and faith receives what he gives. Neither earns anything. A drowning man who grabs a rope has not rescued himself, though he did grab it.

sessions.title: Justification
teaching: Justification is God's verdict that a sinner is right with him. The Reformation's case runs like this. God justifies “the wicked” (Romans 4:5), not the improved, and he does it by counting Christ's righteousness to the one who trusts him, as Abraham's faith was credited to him as righteousness. Justification is a declaration, complete at once, resting on Christ's work outside us rather than on our progress within. Later Lutherans called it the article on which the church stands or falls, and the Augsburg Confession of 1530 set it out in its fourth article. Good works follow as fruit, never as the root. The author stands where the Reformation stood, as Baptists have.

The Catholic answer, set out at the Council of Trent in 1547, does not say that people earn grace; Trent condemned that. It holds that justification includes the renewal of the inner person, grace poured into the heart, so that God's verdict is true of the one he makes righteous, and it points to James: “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). The Orthodox seldom use courtroom language and speak of salvation as healing and union with God. In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics signed a joint declaration confessing that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit, while naming the differences that remain. Other churches have since affirmed it.

Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Adoption
teaching: Justification answers the courtroom; adoption answers the household. A judge can acquit a defendant and still send him home alone. God takes those he justifies into his family. Paul says the Son came “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:5), and he borrows a word from the Roman world, where an adopted heir took the family's name and the full standing of a son. Paul uses it of every believer, daughters as much as sons, because every one is made an heir. The Anglican theologian James Packer, in Knowing God, argued that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel offers, higher even than justification.

Adoption changes how a Christian lives, and most of all how one prays. The Spirit teaches believers to call God by the name Jesus used, Abba, Father, and Paul sets that against a spirit of slavery that falls back into fear. A slave obeys to stay in the house; a child obeys because the house is home. This is where the doctrine of salvation touches some of the deepest wounds people carry. Many have had fathers who were absent, cold or cruel, and the word Father can feel like a door they cannot walk through. Scripture doesn't ask them to picture the father they had. It names the Father they were made for, the one who calls them “children of God” (1 John 3:1).

verse.text: Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him.

care: What if ‘Father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. If your own father was not there, or did not show you love, this verse is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. God's love as a Father is not limited by the father you had. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Sanctification
teaching: Justification is a verdict given once; sanctification is a life made holy over time. The two must never be confused and never separated. If they are confused, a believer's standing with God rises and falls with this week's progress, and assurance dies. If they are separated, grace becomes permission, and the gospel loses its power to change anyone. Paul holds both in one breath: “continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (Philippians 2:12-13). You work out what God works in. The effort is real, but it isn't the source.

Traditions describe the road differently. The Reformed and most Baptists teach progressive sanctification: real growth, never complete in this life, a fight with sin to the end. Wesleyans teach that God can bring a believer in this life to entire sanctification, a heart made perfect in love, though not free from mistakes or temptation. The Keswick movement, from the 1870s, spoke of a deeper surrender that brings rest and victory. The Orthodox speak of theosis, the long healing in which believers become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). Each guards something: honesty about sin, hope of real change, rest in Christ, union with God. Most agree that holiness grows by ordinary means: Scripture, prayer, the Lord's table, the church and time.

sessions.title: Perseverance and assurance
teaching: Can a true believer fall away, and can a believer know they are saved? These are two questions, and they are often confused. On the first, the Reformed tradition teaches the perseverance of the saints: those God truly gives new life he keeps to the end, as Jesus says of his sheep, “No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28). Many Baptists hold it as eternal security, and the Baptist Faith and Message confesses that all true believers endure to the end. Wesleyans, Arminians and Lutherans hold that a real believer can fall away through persistent unbelief, and read the warnings of Hebrews 6 as written to real Christians. Catholic teaching holds that grace can be lost through mortal sin and restored through penance.

Each side reads the other's texts with care. Those who hold perseverance read the warnings as one of the means God uses to keep his people, or as aimed at people who never truly believed. Those who hold that a believer can fall read the promises as sure for all who keep trusting. Assurance is a different matter. John wrote his letter “so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13), and every tradition offers grounds for it: the promise of God, the finished work of Christ, the witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of a changed life. Assurance rests first on Christ, not on the strength of your grip. Anxious consciences need to hear that most of all.

verse.text: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Explaining grace to someone who thinks they must earn it
teaching: Most people you meet already hold a doctrine of salvation, and it is usually some form of earning: be good enough, try hard enough, let the good outweigh the bad. It is the most natural religion in the world, and it sits in church pews as comfortably as anywhere. It also leaves people either proud or crushed, depending on how honest they are about themselves. Jesus told a story to people who trusted in their own righteousness. Two men went up to the temple to pray. One listed his achievements; the other could only ask for mercy. Jesus said of the second, “this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified” (Luke 18:14).

Explaining grace takes less cleverness than you might think. Start where the person is: ask what they think God wants, and listen. Concede what is true in their instinct, because God does care how we live, and holiness is real. Then draw the distinction that changes everything: obedience is the response to being received, not the price of it. A child doesn't earn a place in the family by doing the dishes. Tell your own story of being received, without polish. Borrow the pictures this track has given you, the courtroom, the family, the new birth, the gift, and let the person ask questions. Don't press for a decision or manufacture urgency. Grace pressed on someone stops sounding like grace, and the person who hears it offered freely may carry the question home for years.
